The [Shakers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shakers), formally the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing, began in England and came to New York in 1774 under a leader they called Mother Ann Lee. They lived in celibate communities, held property in common, and believed in the equality of men and women. Their worship included ecstatic dancing, which gave them their nickname.

The movement reached Kentucky in the wake of the great revivals of the early 1800s, including the [Cane Ridge camp meeting](/stories/cane-ridge-meeting-house-and-the-1801-camp-meeting/) of 1801. On New Year's Day 1805, three Shaker missionaries, John Meacham, Issachar Bates, and Benjamin Seth Youngs, left Mount Lebanon, New York, and traveled mostly on foot to Kentucky. In August they found three Kentuckians willing to listen: Elisha Thomas, Samuel Banta, and Henry Banta. They became the state's first Shaker converts.

Believers began moving to Elisha Thomas's 140-acre farm in [Mercer County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mercer_County,_Kentucky). In December 1806, 44 people signed the first family covenant. Two years later they moved to a nearby hilltop they named Pleasant Hill. Most members were farmers, the children and grandchildren of pioneers on the Kentucky River frontier.

The village grew quickly. By 1823 it had 491 Shakers on about 4,500 acres. Over 105 years they built more than 260 structures, including one of Kentucky's earliest municipal water systems. By 1816 they were shipping brooms, cooperage, preserves, and packaged seeds by river to New Orleans, down the Kentucky, Ohio, and Mississippi. They also bred livestock, buying a bull from England together with [Henry Clay](/people/#henry-clay) and building one of America's largest herds of registered Durham Shorthorn cattle.

The Civil War put the pacifist Shakers in a hard spot. They opposed slavery and had admitted African Americans to full membership as early as 1811, but they refused to bear arms, and soldiers from both armies took food and livestock from the village. After the war membership held above 300 for a time, but by 1886 the community was in debt and made up mostly of the very young and the very old. By 1910 Pleasant Hill had closed as an active religious society. The last members deeded their remaining land to a local merchant who agreed to care for them, and the last Pleasant Hill Shaker, Sister Mary Settles, died in 1923. The village became a small town called Shakertown.

## Kentucky today

In 1961 a nonprofit, Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill, formed to buy and restore the buildings. Today visitors can tour the restored village, its farm, and its trails in Mercer County.
